Header:
Date: 2025-06-18

Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Marta Rojas (Stratus Eng Manager), Ethan Cole (SRE), Dr. Sunil Patel (Head of AI)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intro — Jordan from Redwood, and Priya who is our systems SE, will do the deep-dive on autoscaling and capacity planning.
[00:10] Marta: Hi all, thanks. We wanted to walk through how Redwood would handle bursty traffic patterns and what reserved GPU commitments look like for our workloads — especially with long contexts, KV cache behavior, and quantized models.
[00:22] Priya: Great. Quick agenda: we will cover queueing and burst policy models, reserved vs on-demand capacity, continuous batching implications for latency, KV cache hit rate effects, and tips for VPC/on-prem deployments. We'll also call out instrumentation we recommend for capacity planning.
[00:38] Ethan: Sounds good. For context, our production inference peaks around 200 qps at 2k context, but we see sudden bursts up to 1.2k qps during batch jobs and recall windows. P95 latency target is 250ms; P99 ideally under 600ms.
[00:55] Priya: Got it. Two quick clarifications — are those qps per endpoint/model or aggregate? And are bursts short (seconds) or sustained (minutes)?
[01:05] Ethan: It's aggregate across a single model variant, bursts last usually 30s to 5 minutes. Occasional runs last longer when customers kick off bulk imports.
[01:16] Priya: Okay that maps to two different strategies: fast burst absorb (queueing + short lived warmups) and reserved pools for predictable sustained throughput. We'll step through both and share tradeoffs.
[01:30] Jordan: Quick note on terminology: we use 'reserved pool' for dedicated GPUs you commit to, 'burst allowance' for short-term overprovisioning credits that drain, and 'on-demand' for hosted elastic capacity.

[02:00] Topic: Queueing models and latency SLO
[02:05] Priya: The simplest queueing model is M/M/c queuing approximation for homogeneous requests, but real LLM workloads are non-Poisson and cost per request varies strongly with sequence length. So we prefer empirical tail estimations from sampled traces. Two principles: 1) keep queue depth small to avoid head-of-line blocking; 2) prioritize short requests where possible.
[02:36] Marta: How small is 'small'?
[02:38] Priya: For P95 250ms target we aim for queue times under 50ms. That means sizing workers so utilization stays below ~65-70% under expected load, because queuing delay balloons near high utilization.
[02:50] Ethan: So that suggests more reserved GPUs than naive throughput calc.
[02:54] Priya: Exactly. Rough calc: take effective tokens/sec per GPU at your typical context lengths and target utilization 65%. We can share a spreadsheet model. Jordan will attach it.

[03:20] Topic: Burst policies and warm pools
[03:23] Priya: For short bursts (under ~2-3 minutes) we recommend a hybrid: a small warm pool of kept-alive instances that are fast to spin up and a burst allowance which lets hosted elastic traffic overflow to on-demand capacity. Warm pools are cheaper than full reserved GPUs because they can be smaller or use lightweight instances with smaller KV caches.
[03:46] Marta: What's the warm-up time for a model with 16k context?
[03:49] Priya: For a full model with 16k context on an A100-class instance, cold startup (cold kernels + model load) can be 20-60s depending on quant and filesystem caching. If you have a kept-warm process with KV cache initialized it can be under 5-8s. But good to plan for variability.
[04:10] Ethan: Is there a way to pre-warm just KVs and not the whole model?
[04:13] Priya: Yes — Redwood supports prefix/KV cache pre-warming. You can seed slices of typical prompt prefixes so the KV cache hits on first requests. For very long contexts we also support lazy KV population and streaming so the initial tokens can return earlier while the rest warms.

[04:40] Topic: Reserved GPUs vs Dedicated burst pools
[04:42] Priya: Reserved GPUs give you predictable tail-latency and unit cost. But you should size them for baseline plus expected steady-state throughput. For bursty traffic, combine reserved with a small dedicated burst pool — cheaper than scaling reserved quota, and you pay only when the pool is used.
[05:00] Jordan: Note: reserved pool pricing has volume discounts and SLA credits. We'll share a tailored quote.

[05:20] Topic: Batching & continuous batching effects
[05:22] Priya: Continuous batching increases throughput but introduces batching latency. Redwood's serving runtime has adaptive batching that aims to keep batching delay under a configurable threshold. Tradeoff knob: increase batch window to improve GPU utilization (lower cost) at the expense of added jitter. For deterministic latency we recommend tight batch windows + more workers.
[05:45] Dr. Patel: For medical use-cases we can't have unpredictable tail latency. We need strict P99 bounds.
[05:51] Priya: In that case prioritize reserved capacity and tight batching windows and run controlled load tests to get empirical P99 numbers. We also suggest quantization profiles that preserve determinism — some lossy quant paths can have variance.

[06:20] Topic: KV cache impact on throughput and cost
[06:23] Priya: KV cache greatly reduces compute per token for multi-turn chat, especially with long histories. Key knobs: cache segment size, eviction policy, and cross-request sharing. With high KV hit rates you can support 2-4x more sustained qps on the same GPU. But cache population and eviction cause variability; we instrument with hit-rate histograms and per-request token-saved metrics.
[06:50] Ethan: Any guidance on cache sizing for 16k contexts?
[06:53] Priya: Start with storing full KV windows for active sessions and use MRU eviction for low churn. For 16k contexts with many users, consider sharded KV cache across multiple workers rather than one monolithic cache per process. We'll provide examples in runbook.

[07:20] Topic: Quantization tradeoffs
[07:22] Priya: 8-bit and 4-bit quantization reduce memory and increase throughput. But effects on latency are nuanced: smaller models fit more efficiently into GPU memory allowing larger batch sizes, which may increase batch latency but lower per-token cost. Also watch for quality regressions on sensitive prompts; always run evals.
[07:45] Dr. Patel: We have regulatory need to audit model change effects. Do you support A/B rollouts?
[07:50] Jordan: Yes — Redwood Console supports canary rollouts, A/B with traffic splits, and quality regressions tied to prompt suites. We log inputs/outputs for evals under customer-controlled retention windows and can integrate with your audit pipeline.

[08:10] Topic: VPC/on-prem considerations
[08:12] Priya: For VPC/private deployments the main differences are networking (no public ELB), image/cached model distribution, and cold-start behavior. On-prem we see longer cold starts when models are pulled over slower storage; mitigation: local caching tier or pre-pulling models to nodes. Also KMS integration requires special routing for HSMs — we document patterns in the private deployment guide.
[08:39] Marta: If we run private deployment, can we still use Redwood's burst allowance?
[08:43] Priya: You can configure hybrid modes: a private control plane with ability to route overflow to Redwood-hosted pools, but that requires network egress and an agreement — it's common for regulated customers who allow limited outbound.

[09:05] Topic: Observability & capacity planning instrumentation
[09:08] Priya: Key metrics: per-model tokens/sec, per-GPU utilization, queue depth histograms, KV hit rate, batch size distribution, cold-start counts, and tail-latency percentiles by request size. Also export traces for long-running requests. Redwood ships these to your telemetry or can forward to Datadog/Prometheus.
[09:30] Ethan: Can we get per-tenant isolation metrics?
[09:33] Priya: Yes — Redwood exposes per-route and token-level breakdowns including cost attribution and latency. Useful for chargeback and SLO enforcement.

[10:00] Mid-call: demo references and links
[10:03] Jordan: I'll drop the benchmark spreadsheet and a sample runbook to the thread: https://redwood.example.com/docs/autoscale-runbook and an example benchmark: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/16k-kv

[10:15] Deep technical exchanges (selected excerpts)
[10:20] Priya: On sustained 1k qps at 2k context, an A100-80GB with optimized kernels + 4-bit quant can do roughly X tokens/sec depending on replication and batch windows — again we should run your exact samples.
[10:37] Ethan: When you say X tokens/sec, do you mean steady-state typing speed or including prefix generation?
[10:40] Priya: Steady-state. Prefix generation costs extra, but with KV cache it amortizes. For tail-latency planning, assume worst-case token counts per request to avoid surprises.

[11:05] Marta: How do you handle overload? Drop requests or queue?
[11:09] Priya: Policy-based: we support adaptive shedding (reject with friendly error), prioritization (short requests, retries), queue bounds with TTL, and soft-degrading to lower-capacity model variants. For critical flows, you can set hard SLOs that route only to reserved pools.
[11:28] Dr. Patel: Is there support for model fallback that keeps format consistent?
[11:31] Priya: Yes — automatic fallback to quantized or smaller model variants with same output schema; Redwood's tool calling and function spec ensures structured outputs remain stable. We recommend upfront schema validations in your client.

[12:00] Discussion: Cost modeling
[12:03] Jordan: Cost is combination of reserved committed hours, on-demand burst hours, and per-token charges for hosted. For dedicated pools you pay for GPU hours; for hosted on-demand you pay more per unit but avoid reserved commitments. We'll give a cost-per-qps model in the spreadsheet.
[12:22] Ethan: Any thoughts on hybrid pricing for temp spikes?
[12:25] Jordan: We offer burst credits and pre-paid burst packs for enterprise customers — cheaper than purely on-demand. We'll include options in the quote.

[12:45] Customer concerns and clarifications
[12:47] Marta: We have strict audit windows — how long do you keep traces? Can the retention be customer-controlled?
[12:52] Jordan: Yes, retention is configurable; for Private deployments you control retention entirely. For hosted, Redwood offers configurable levels (30/90/365 days) and data export.

[13:05] Performance test plan
[13:08] Priya: Actionable plan: 1) Customer provides representative trace (Ethan will share), 2) Priya will configure benchmark harness to replay at target qps with latency capture, 3) run tests with: reserved pool baseline, reserved + warm pool, reserved + burst allowance, and pure hosted on-demand. We'll measure P50/P95/P99, queue depth, KV hit-rate, and cold-start counts.
[13:28] Ethan: We'll anonymize traces and strip PHI before sharing.

[13:35] Troubleshooting and gotchas
[13:37] Priya: Watch out for head-of-line blocking when mixing very long and short requests. Mitigations: separate routers (route short vs long), request size thresholds, or priority queues. Also pre-warm kernels on new nodes to avoid runtime jit overheads.
[13:58] Marta: How deterministic are quantized kernels across hardware families?
[14:01] Priya: Slight variance exists; our compile step picks kernels per hardware and we recommend per-hardware validation. For strict determinism pick the same instance type and quant profile for the pool.

[14:20] Recap and commitments
[14:22] Jordan: Recap: we'll share runbook, pricing options, and benchmark spreadsheet. Priya will run the perf tests once we get traces. Customer will provide SLOs and traffic distributions. Also flagged: KV pre-warm strategy and warm pool sizing.
[14:40] Marta: Good. Also want to know expected cold-start SLA if we use private with pre-pulled images.
[14:45] Priya: Typical private pre-pulled image starts under 10s if model artifacts are on local NVMe; on slower NFS it could be 40-90s. We'll add guidance to the runbook.

[14:58] Final Q&A and close
[15:00] Ethan: One last: any recommendations for our CI/CD to avoid rollouts that break latency?
[15:03] Priya: Yes — gate rollouts on canary perf tests in your CI that run a few thousand synthetic requests measuring P99. Also tie rollback to automated alerts when tail-latency exceeds threshold.
[15:18] Jordan: We'll send the sample canary jobs and a Jenkins/GitHub actions example.
[15:25] Marta: Thanks — this was super helpful.
[15:28] Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll send the materials and follow up with dates for the perf run.
